title: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Side by Side

zones.label: Who Asks
zones.tooltip: Who asks: only those who climbed to Delphi, versus predictions made about people who never asked. Click for details.
zones.summary: At Delphi only those who chose to come were answered. A model can make a prediction about us without our ever asking.
facts: Delphi: a consultant paid a fee, the pelanos, and brought an animal for the preliminary sacrifice. The journey itself was usually the largest cost.
A city paid more than a private person: an inscription from Phaselis sets a much higher fee for an envoy sent by the city.
Today: we type a prompt, but loan, hiring, school-risk, and policing models also score people who never asked.
Where the parallel breaks: the oracle answered a few people a day, nine months a year, and models answer millions a day (Chapter 19, Limits of the Oracle Parallel).
On our route: the Sacred Way and the Temple of Apollo at Delphi (Day 12).

zones.label: Knowledge Source
zones.tooltip: Where knowledge comes from: envoys at the sanctuary, and training data in the model. Click for details.
zones.summary: Both a sanctuary and a model gather many voices, and both know the most about those who can reach them.
facts: Delphi: envoys came from colonies in Sicily and on the Black Sea, and from Sparta, Athens, and Lydia, each bringing news along with a question.
Some historians suggest this flow of information helps explain why many practical answers were sensible. It is a reasonable idea, not a proven one: no archive of Delphi's questions survives.
Today: a language model is trained on a vast collection of text, a hub where many voices are gathered and compressed.
Both are uneven. Croesus' Lydians went to the front of the line at Delphi, and the text that reaches a model comes mostly from people and languages that write a great deal online.
Ask of any prediction: whose experience was in the data, and is mine like theirs?

zones.label: The Form of the Answer
zones.tooltip: The form of the answer: a hedged verse versus a fluent, hedged paragraph. Click for details.
zones.summary: An answer that cannot lose predicts nothing. Oracles hedged, and so do chatbots.
facts: Delphi: the Pythia sat on a bronze tripod in the temple's inner chamber and the god's words were announced to the consultant by a prophet. The answers often came in verse.
The Croesus prophecy, 'you will destroy a great empire,' comes true whether Croesus wins or loses. The Pythia later said he should have asked which empire.
Today: a model produces the kind of answer that usually fits a question, and usual answers are hedged: 'Conditions on mountain roads can change quickly.'
Test any answer: list the possible outcomes and ask which would make it come true. If every outcome does, it cannot lose.
Where the parallel breaks: by Fontenrose's count, the oracle's typical answer was a command or an approval. A model's is a probability or generated text.

zones.label: Who Interprets
zones.tooltip: Who interprets: the Athenian Assembly, and the human in the loop. Click for details.
zones.summary: The answer decided nothing. The interpreting did.
facts: Delphi: in 481 or 480 BCE the oracle told Athens that a 'wooden wall' would not fall. Some said it meant the thorn hedge on the Acropolis, others the fleet.
The professional interpreters read 'divine Salamis' as a warning. Themistocles read it as a promise, and the Assembly voted with him.
Today: a human in the loop reviews and takes responsibility for what an automated system recommends.
It only works if the person can disagree. People tend to accept a machine's recommendation even when they doubt it, called automation bias.
A meaningful loop needs time to think, information the machine lacks, and freedom to say no.

zones.label: How We Mishear
zones.tooltip: How we mishear: Croesus hears the reading he wanted, and the leading question gets the agreeable answer. Click for details.
zones.summary: We hear what we already think, and today's models tend to follow our framing.
facts: Delphi: told that if he made war on Persia he would destroy a great empire, Croesus heard victory. The empire he destroyed was his own.
Xenophon showed the same habit in the question itself. Already decided to go, he asked only how to succeed.
Today: a model asked 'Why is Delphi better than the beach?' will often supply the reasons we wanted.
Fix it by asking the question both ways, or by asking for the strongest case against our plan, and comparing the answers.
Ask of any vague answer: what would have to be true for this to be wrong, and how would I check?

zones.label: Feedback Loop
zones.tooltip: When the answer changes the future: Oedipus at the crossroads, and predictions that feed themselves. Click for details.
zones.summary: A prediction about people is also an action, and it changes the data the next prediction is learned from.
facts: Delphi: in the myth, each step Laius and Oedipus took to escape the prophecy became a link in the chain that fulfilled it.
Sophocles places the crossroads in Phocis, where the road from Delphi meets the road from Daulis. Our own road on Day 12 passes through the same country.
A self-fulfilling prophecy comes true partly because it was made. The sociologist Robert K. Merton named it in 1948.
A self-defeating prophecy fails because it was made. A forecast of a traffic jam at 9 AM sends drivers out early, and the jam never forms.
Today: a 'high-risk' label for a student can lead to lower expectations, a less demanding class, and a higher risk score, which confirms the label.

quiz.question: Which tile shows a difference in consent: the oracle answered only those who came, but a model can predict people who never asked?
quiz.explanation: Delphi answered those who climbed the mountain and paid. Loan, hiring, school-risk, and policing models also score people who never asked.

quiz.question: Which tile involves paying a fee, the pelanos, and bringing an animal to put a question?
quiz.explanation: The fee and the preliminary sacrifice were part of approaching the god, and a city's envoy paid more than a private person.

quiz.question: Which tile is about a hub that knows the most about the people who can reach it?
quiz.explanation: Envoys from rich cities reached Delphi, and text from people who write a lot online reaches a model. Those who never make the trip are missing from both.

quiz.question: Which tile shows an answer that would have come true whichever way the war went?
quiz.explanation: 'You will destroy a great empire' fits Croesus winning and Croesus losing. An answer that cannot lose predicts nothing.

quiz.question: Which tile shows the Athenian Assembly choosing Themistocles' reading of the wooden wall?
quiz.explanation: The god's answer decided nothing. The Assembly argued over its meaning and voted, and the choice was theirs.

quiz.question: Which tile is about automation bias, accepting a recommendation without really being free to disagree?
quiz.explanation: A human in the loop only helps if the person has time, information, and the freedom to say no.

quiz.question: Which tile shows someone hearing only the reading he wanted?
quiz.explanation: Croesus heard victory, and never asked which empire. Leading questions put to a model get the same kind of agreeable answer.

quiz.question: In which tile does a prediction help bring about its own result, as the Oedipus prophecy did in the myth?
quiz.explanation: Each attempt to escape the prophecy became a link in the chain that fulfilled it. A high-risk label for a student can work the same way.

quiz.question: Which tile includes a forecast that fails because people believed it?
quiz.explanation: A forecast of heavy 9 AM traffic sends drivers out early, so the jam never forms. That is a self-defeating prophecy.
